name: No Balance Left
description: Alisa has a shopping card with an initial balance of $$$h$$$. There are $$$n$$$ types of products in a supermarket. A product of type $$$i$$$ costs $$$c_i$$$, and Alisa can buy any number of products of each type. There are also $$$m$$$ rebate activities. The $$$j$$$-th activity applies to a purchase if its total cost is at least $$$a_j$$$ and gives a rebate of $$$b_j$$$. For each purchase, Alisa performs the following operations: She chooses one or more products whose total cost $$$x$$$ does not exceed the current balance on her card and pays $$$x$$$ using the card. Among all rebate activities that apply to this purchase, the one with the largest rebate takes effect and its rebate is added to the card balance. If no rebate activity applies, no rebate is added. For every $$$h$$$ from $$$1$$$ to $$$s$$$, determine whether Alisa can make the balance on her card equal to $$$0$$$ after finitely many purchases.
input_specification: The first line contains three integers $$$n$$$, $$$m$$$, and $$$s$$$ ($$$1 \le n, m, s \le 125\,000$$$) — the number of product types, the number of rebate activities, and the maximum initial balance to consider, respectively. The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_n$$$ ($$$1 \le c_i \le 125\,000$$$) — the price of a product of each type. The $$$i$$$-th of the next $$$m$$$ lines contains two integers $$$a_i$$$ and $$$b_i$$$ ($$$1 \le a_i, b_i \le 125\,000$$$) — the spending threshold and the rebate of the $$$i$$$-th activity, respectively. It is guaranteed that $$$a_1 \lt a_2 \lt \cdots \lt a_m$$$ and $$$b_1 \lt b_2 \lt \cdots \lt b_m$$$.
output_specification: Print $$$s$$$ lines. For each $$$i$$$ ($$$1 \le i \le s$$$), print " YES " if Alisa can make the balance on her card equal to $$$0$$$ when its initial balance is $$$i$$$, and print " NO " otherwise. You can output the answer in any case (upper or lower). For example, the strings " yEs ", " yes ", " Yes ", and " YES " will be recognized as positive responses.

approach_summary: Define state dp[mask][i] capturing the subset of visited/chosen elements. Transition by iterating over valid unset bits in O(2^N × N) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 2248G — No Balance Left [450. Bitmask DP]
topic_editorial.summary: Bitmask DP state compression over subsets.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Because the dimension $N$ is small ($N \le 20$), each subset of chosen or visited elements can be encoded compactly into a single bitmask integer $0 \le \text{mask} < 2^N$. The optimal substructure property guarantees that to extend a subset $\text{mask}$, we only need to know the current subset and optionally the last added element.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: State Definition
Define $dp[\text{mask}]$ (or $dp[\text{mask}][u]$ if the last visited element matters) as:
- $dp[\text{mask}] = $ the optimal value obtainable using the subset of elements represented by the bitmask $\text{mask}$.

### Step 2: Base Cases
- Initialize all DP states to a sentinel value (e.g. $\infty$ for minimization, or $-\infty$ for maximization).
- Base state: $dp[0] = 0$ (empty configuration has cost zero).

### Step 3: Recurrence Relation & Transitions
For every mask from $0$ to $2^N - 1$:
If the state $dp[\text{mask}]$ is reachable:
For every element $i \in [0, N-1]$ such that the $i$-th bit is NOT set in $\text{mask}$ ($(\text{mask} \mathbin{\&} (1 \ll i)) == 0$):
$$\text{next\_mask} = \text{mask} \mid (1 \ll i)$$
$$dp[\text{next\_mask}] = \text{opt}\big(dp[\text{next\_mask}], dp[\text{mask}] + \text{cost}(\text{mask}, i)\big)$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
The final answer is stored in $dp[(1 \ll N) - 1]$, which corresponds to all $N$ elements being chosen.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(2^N \cdot N)$
  There are $2^N$ total bitmasks. From each mask, we iterate over at most $N$ possible next bits to transition. For $N = 20$, $2^{20} \cdot 20 \approx 2 \times 10^7$ operations, which easily runs in $\approx 0.15$ seconds.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(2^N)$
  Storing the DP table for all $2^N$ configurations requires $2^{20} \times 8$ bytes $\approx 8\text{ MB}$ of memory, well below 256 MB.
